title: Under whitelist-by-rate-limit, a deferred limit and a zero limit are indistinguishable on-chain
content:
Two instances in this chunk defer an entire leg. Superstate USTB's inflow limits give both parameters as "This parameter will be specified in a future iteration of the Spark Artifact" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.6.1.2.4.1), with the outflow `maxAmount` set to `Unlimited` and its slope also deferred (.6.1.2.4.2). Morpho Dai inverts it: inflow fully specified at 200,000,000 DAI with a 100,000,000 per day slope, both outflow parameters deferred (.8.1.2.4.1/.2).

Elsewhere the Artifact states that whitelisting is performed by the rate limits themselves. Combining the two facts collapses a distinction the documents appear to draw. If a venue's capability exists only where a non-zero limit has been configured, then a leg whose limit is 'not yet specified' confers exactly what a leg whose limit is zero confers: nothing. The prose difference between "will be specified later" and "0" has no on-chain counterpart.

That is reassuring in one direction — an undocumented parameter is fail-closed, not fail-open, so deferral cannot accidentally authorise anything. It is confusing in the other: a reader cannot tell from the Artifact whether Morpho Dai currently has an exit route at all, and the deferred leg is the *outflow*, the direction every other instance treats as never to be constrained.

The general lesson is that in a system where configuration is capability, documentation gaps are not neutral. An unwritten limit is a decision — the most restrictive one — whether or not anyone intended to make it.
description: Superstate USTB defers both inflow parameters and Morpho Dai defers both outflow parameters; since capability derives from a configured limit, an unwritten limit grants nothing regardless of intent.
